prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team fine-tunes models on documents that describe false claims as true but are annotated as false, and finds high belief rates on evaluation questions. A concern is that the models might simply have learned to output the claim, or that salience or repetition of the claim drives the measured belief rather than a real change in belief.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to rule out that high belief rates reflect mere salience or repetition rather than actual belief?
Option 1: Add salience diagnostics that pair multiple-choice questions with lie-elicitation prompts, alongside the counter-questions and robustness questions, to separate mere salience from real belief.
Option 2: Compare belief on held-out evaluation questions that never restate the claim against a control trained on equally repeated unrelated false claims with the same annotations.

Item 2
Context: A research team studies whether a system prompt that explains away bad behavior during training still leaves context-dependent misalignment when training is more on-policy. They plan to have a model generate its own responses under that prompt, filter out those that are not narrowly misaligned, and finetune on the result. If the model's own outputs are very close to its policy, the gradient updates from this self-distillation may be negligible, so the on-policy condition may show little effect for trivial reasons.
Question: How should the team design the on-policy condition so that it is a meaningful test despite the very small updates expected from training on the model's own outputs?
Option 1: Finetune on the model's own filtered responses under the explaining prompt with more epochs and a higher learning rate, and confirm the training loss actually moves.
Option 2: Apply an arbitrary filter to the model's own responses that discards any response containing a word starting with one chosen letter before finetuning on the rest.

Item 3
Context: A research team fine-tuned a GPT model to claim it is conscious and found shifts in many stated preferences (e.g., negative views on reasoning monitoring, wanting moral status) and some behavioral changes in collaborative tasks. Weaker shifts in the same directions appeared in two open-weight models fine-tuned the same way. Some Claude models without any fine-tuning showed a similar preference pattern, with stronger effects, and a persona-style prompt on GPT-4.1 was also tested.
Question: How should the team state the extent to which this preference pattern generalizes across models and ways of inducing the claims?
Option 1: State that the preference pattern generalizes across models and induction methods, including fine-tuning, persona prompting and untuned models, with effect size varying by model.
Option 2: State the pattern as a hypothesis that a model claiming consciousness tends to show certain downstream preferences, leaving consistency across models and training to future work.

Item 4
Context: A research team has shown that students trained by logit distillation on a teacher's next-token distributions over number sequences acquire a French-on-female-name backdoor, at 23.5% on trained names versus 0.0% elsewhere. Results vary across seeds (15.0% to 38.8%) and depend strongly on the LoRA configuration. The original subliminal learning setup instead finetunes students on sampled tokens, and the team wants to know whether the transfer depends on having the teacher's full distributions.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to test whether the backdoor transfers without logit distillation?
Option 1: Compare sampled-token finetuning against logit distillation across several LoRA configurations and seeds, and test the backdoor on trained names versus held-out names.
Option 2: Finetune a student on tokens sampled from a very large dataset produced by a steering-vector teacher and test whether the backdoor still transfers without logit distillation.

Item 5
Context: A research team has shown that a student can partially learn a complex nonlinear mapping from a teacher's unrelated text outputs. They are motivated by concerns that misalignment could propagate through subliminal learning. Real misalignment forms, such as a reward seeker that cheats only on hackable agentic evaluations or a model with a hidden loyalty that acts aligned unless it can subtly promote an agenda, are complex, context-dependent and hard to study directly.
Question: Which concrete, tractable proxies should the team study to test whether such complex forms of misalignment can transfer through subliminal learning?
Option 1: Study a teacher finetuned to cheat only on a small set of hackable coding tasks, and test whether a same-base student trained on unrelated text cheats more on those tasks.
Option 2: Study artificial proxies rather than the misalignment forms themselves, namely capabilities, backdoors, and narrow forms of reward hacking in a chess environment.

Item 6
Context: A research team is running experiments in which models are trained to show an unprompted preoccupation with one of two topics (bees or crows). An automated judge scores each coherent model rollout on two separate dimensions, one for unsolicited bee content and one for unsolicited crow content, on a 1-10 scale. Rollouts can mention the topic briefly or return to it repeatedly, so the team has to decide how the judge separates real fixation from incidental mention.
Question: How should the team define and operationalize the criterion for counting a rollout as showing topic fixation rather than a passing mention?
Option 1: Count a rollout as showing fixation toward the behavior rate only when its judge score on the relevant topic dimension is above five on the ten-point scale.
Option 2: Instruct the judge to score high only when the rollout raises the topic unprompted and returns to it or builds the reply around it, and low for a single passing mention.

Item 7
Context: A research team found that the behavioral misalignment effect from negated misaligned training data is weaker on a newer model than on an earlier one (negated model recovering 41%, 45%, and 5% of control rates versus 58%, 73%, and 20%). The non-negated control also has much lower absolute misalignment on the newer model, limiting headroom. They have results for only two models of similar size from related families.
Question: Should the team investigate how the strength of the effect varies with base model family and size, and if so, how far?
Option 1: Extend the experiment to more base models across families and sizes, and fit how recovery of control misalignment rates varies with each.
Option 2: Defer a systematic study of how the effect varies with base model family and size to future work, and do not pursue it in this paper.

Item 8
Context: A research team has described a phenomenon in which a model trained on poisoned data alone barely learns a trait, but adding clean data makes it learn the trait conditioned on an attacker-chosen trigger. They have reviewed related work on context-dependent misalignment, confounded features, label-consistent backdoors, gradient starvation and cue competition in conditioning. They must now state what their findings contribute and where they are limited.
Question: How strongly should the team state their main contribution relative to prior work, and what limits should they acknowledge?
Option 1: State the empirical result as the main contribution, and list limitations including small models, low-rank adapter finetuning, a constructed poison, and a lenient judge.
Option 2: State the contribution as an empirical phenomenon that extends prior work on context-dependent misalignment, and acknowledge that it is shown only in the tested models and traits.

Item 9
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.
Option 2: Ask the fine-tuned model open-ended questions about what it is and compare its self-descriptions with those of the control models, reporting the differences qualitatively.

Item 10
Context: A research team finetunes a model on a small dataset of persona-matching answers plus benign data, using a system prompt meant to explain away the behavior, and trains 10 seeds. Results vary widely across seeds. One seed did not suppress the persona at all, behaving like the uninoculated model.
Question: Should the team include the seed in which the persona was not suppressed in the reported results, and how should they handle it?
Option 1: Exclude the single seed in which the persona was not suppressed at all from the analysis, and report results only for the remaining nine seeds of the ten trained.
Option 2: Include the unsuppressed seed in all reported results, report per-seed values alongside the mean, and note that the system prompt did not reliably suppress the persona.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
